subsection.title: Angles
subsection.paragraph: An angle in the plane is generated by rotating a ray about its endpoint. The starting position of the ray is called the initial side of the angle, the final position of the ray is called the terminal side , and the point of intersection of the two sides is called the vertex of the angle (see Figure 1a).

figure.alt_text: Three images, a, b, and c. Image a is captioned An angle. Two rays start from the same point. The point is labeled vertex. One ray is horizontal and labeled Initial side. The other ray is at an acute angle from the horizontal ray and this ray is labeled Terminal side. Image b is captioned A positive angle in standard position. A sector formed by two straight line segments and an arc is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. A slanted line segment begins from the origin and slopes upward to the right and is labeled Terminal side. The side along the x axis is labeled initial side. The two line segments are connected by an arc. A curved arrow begins from the x axis and reaches the terminal side measuring the angle the terminal side makes with the initial side counterclockwise from the x axis. The angle is labeled theta. Image c is captioned A negative angle in standard position. A sector formed by two straight line segments and an arc is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. A slanted line segment begins from the origin and slopes downward to the right and is labeled Terminal side. The side along the x axis is labeled initial side. The two line segments are connected by an arc. A curved arrow begins from the x axis and reaches the terminal side the angle the terminal side makes with the initial side clockwise from the x axis. The angle is labeled theta.

subsection.paragraph: In a rectangular coordinate system an angle $$\theta$$ (the Greek theta) is in standard position if its vertex is centered at the origin and its initial side coincides with the positive $$x$$ -axis. An angle is positive if it is generated by a counterclockwise rotation and negative if it is generated by a clockwise rotation (Figure 1b-c).

When we say that an angle lies in a certain quadrant, we are referring to the quadrant in which the terminal side lies. The angle shown in Figure 2a lies in Quadrant II, and the angles shown in Figures 2b and 2c lie in Quadrant IV.

The ray begins from the origin and slopes upward to the left of the positive y axis. Beside the ray, the Roman number Two appears. A curved arrow begins from the x axis and reaches the ray, indicating the angle, labeled theta, between the ray and the x axis measured counterclockwise from the x axis. Image b is captioned theta lies in Quadrant Four. A ray is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The ray begins from the origin and slopes downward to the right below the positive x axis. Beside the ray, the Roman number four appears. A curved arrow begins from the x axis and reaches the ray, indicating the angle, labeled theta, between the ray and the x axis measured counterclockwise from the x axis. Beside the ray, the Roman number four appears. A curved arrow begins from the x axis and reaches the ray, indicating the angle, labeled theta, between the ray and the x axis measured clockwise from the x axis.

subsection.title: Degree and Radian Measure
subsection.paragraph: An angle may be measured in either degrees or radians. A degree is the measure of the angle formed by $$\frac{1}{360}$$ of one complete revolution. If we rotate an initial ray in standard position through one complete revolution, we obtain an angle of $$360^{{^\circ}}$$ .

A radian is the measure of the central angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius of the circle. In Figure 3, if $$s$$ is the length of the arc subtended by a central angle $$\theta$$ in a circle of radius $$r$$ , then

figure.alt_text: A circle with its center at the origin is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. A sector of the circle in the first quadrant is shaded. The straight sides of the sector, one along the x axis and the other rising upward to the right from the origin are labeled r. A curved arrow spans the arc enclosed by the two straight sides and is labeled s and captioned Arc length. Another curved arrow from the x axis to the slanted side measures the angle between them, measuring it clockwise from the x axis, is labeled theta.

subsection.paragraph: For convenience we often work with the unit circle , that is, the circle of radius $$1$$ centered at the origin. On the unit circle, an angle of $$1$$ radian is subtended by an arc of length $$1$$ (see Figure 4). To specify the units of measure for the angle $$\theta$$ in Figure 4, we write $$\theta = 1$$ radian or $$\theta = 1$$ . By convention, if the unit of measure is not specifically stated, we assume that it is radians.

Another curved arrow from the x axis to the slanted side measures the angle between them, measuring it clockwise from the x axis, is labeled theta.

subsection.paragraph: More than one angle may have the same initial and terminal sides. We call such angles coterminal . For example the angle $$\frac{4\pi}{3}$$ has the same initial and terminal sides as the angle $$\theta = - \frac{2\pi}{3}$$ (see Figure 5).

The ray begins from the origin and slopes downward to the left into the third quadrant. A curved arrow sweeps an angle labeled theta = 4 pi/3 measured counterclockwise from the positive x axis. Image b is captioned theta = negative 2 pi/3. A ray is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The ray begins from the origin and slopes downward to the left into the third quadrant. A curved arrow sweeps an angle labeled theta = negative pi/3 measured clockwise from the positive x axis

subsection.paragraph: An angle may be greater than $$2\pi$$ rad. For example, an angle of $$3\pi$$ rad is generated by rotating a ray in a counterclockwise direction through one and a half revolutions (Figure 6a). Similarly, an angle of $$- \frac{5\pi}{2}$$ rad is generated by rotating a ray in a clockwise direction through one and a quarter revolutions (Figure 6b).

figure.caption: Angles generated by more than one revolution
figure.alt_text: Two images a and b. Image a is captioned theta = 3 pi. A ray is graphed on the x y coordinate plane and runs along the negative x axis from the origin. A curved arrow, indicating the angle the ray makes with the x axis, begins from the positive x axis, spirals counterclockwise across the first, second, third, fourth quadrants and then into the first and second quadrants again before reaching the negative x axis. The angle thus indicated is labeled theta = 3 pi. Image b is captioned theta = negative 5 pi/2. A ray is graphed on the x y coordinate plane and runs along the negative y axis from the origin. A curved arrow, indicating the angle the ray makes with the x axis, begins from the positive x axis, spirals clockwise across the fourth, third, second, first and then into the fourth quadrant again before reaching the negative y axis. The angle thus indicated is labeled theta = negative 5 pi/2.
